title: Bangladesh signs China investment pact as work starts on China-funded Mongla port jetties
dek: Prime Minister Tarique Rahman laid the foundation stone for Tk 4,068 crore container jetties paid for mostly by China Exim Bank, signed an investment memorandum with China Railway Construction Corporation, and promised road, power and gas links north to Panchagarh, near north Bengal.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Bangladesh's Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Thursday laid the foundation stone for two container jetties at Mongla port, a Tk 4,068 crore project paid for mostly with a loan from the Export-Import Bank of China and built by a Chinese state-owned contractor. Mongla, Bangladesh's second-largest seaport, sits on the Pasur river beside the Sundarbans, close to the West Bengal border.

China is lending about Tk 3,593 crore, nearly nine-tenths of the cost, and Bangladesh is paying about Tk 475 crore. The project is meant to give Mongla its first dedicated container-handling jetties and to add about 400,000 containers (measured in twenty-foot equivalent units, or TEUs) a year of capacity. That is more than ten times the number of containers the port handled last year. At the same visit, Bangladesh signed a memorandum on wider investment with China Railway Construction Corporation (CRCC), a Chinese state-owned group, and Rahman promised road, power and gas links running north from Mongla towards Panchagarh, the district that borders north Bengal.

## What happened

Rahman attended two programmes at the port: the signing of an investment memorandum and the foundation-stone ceremony for the jetties. The memorandum, between Invest Bangladesh, the government's investment promotion agency, and CRCC, was signed by Saleh Ahmed of Invest Bangladesh and by Li Chongyang, whom one report described as chairman of CRCC's subsidiary China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation (CCECC). Under it, the two sides will "explore" investment in energy, industrial and green infrastructure, transport and logistics, and skills training. No figure, project list or timetable has been published, and the memorandum does not by itself commit either side to any investment. Rahman later met a Chinese delegation led by CRCC's chairman, Dai Hegen, and urged more Chinese investment, especially in Mongla, reports said.

The project, formally called "Expansion and Modernisation of Facilities at Mongla Port", covers:

- two new container jetties, numbered 10 and 11, with a combined quay length of 368 metres
- a container yard, a container delivery yard and a yard for dangerous goods
- 49 pieces of cargo-handling equipment, which the port authority expects to move more than 30 containers an hour

The engineering, procurement and construction contractor is China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation (CCECC), a subsidiary of CRCC, according to reports. The port authority's chairman, Rear Admiral Arif Ahmed Mustafa, said construction would begin after the ceremony. One report said that the project is due to be finished by December 2028.

## How China is paying for it

The China-Bangladesh joint communiqué issued on 26 June, at the end of Rahman's visit to Beijing, lists the "Mongla Port Facilities Modernization and Expansion Project" among the projects the two governments agreed to take forward. The loan agreement followed on 10 October. The loan is for 2.404 billion yuan, about $336 million. One report gave the terms as 2% interest, repayable over 20 years including a five-year grace period.

## Background

Mongla is a small port by regional standards. It handled 29,700 TEUs of containers and 1.22 crore tonnes of cargo in the year to June 2026, according to Mongla Port Authority figures cited in one report. Container traffic rose 38% on the year before.

India has its own stake in the port. Under a 2018 agreement on the use of Chattogram and Mongla ports, Indian goods can be shipped through both ports to and from India's north-eastern states. India also agreed to finance a much larger upgrade of Mongla through a line of credit. In December 2022, one report said that the "Upgradation of Mongla Port" project was estimated at Tk 6,014 crore, with Tk 4,459 crore of it to come from the Indian credit line. That project was also meant to add 400,000 TEUs of container capacity, but another report from November 2022 said work had not started eight years after the loan agreement was signed. The Declaration could not establish the current status of the Indian-funded project, and neither government mentioned it on Thursday.

The jetties are one of several Chinese projects in Bangladesh's south-west and north. On Wednesday, Liu Haixing, head of the Chinese Communist Party's International Department, told a roundtable in Dhaka that work was "advancing steadily" on a Mongla Port industrial park and on a plan to restore the Teesta river, which flows into Bangladesh from north Bengal.

## What it means for India and Bengal

The project puts a Chinese state-owned company in charge of building and equipping a port near the Indian border and the Sundarbans, the mangrove delta that India and Bangladesh share. There is no public sign that China will operate the jetties: the port authority, a Bangladeshi government body, is the owner. But the equipment, the contractor and most of the money are Chinese, and repayments to China Exim Bank will run into the 2040s.

There are three concrete issues for India:

- **Competition and transit.** Mongla, like the Kolkata and Haldia docks, serves shipping at the head of the Bay of Bengal. Modern container jetties would make it more attractive to shipping lines, and Indian transit cargo can use the port under the 2018 agreement.
- **The Indian-funded project.** The new jetties promise roughly the same container capacity as the larger Indian line-of-credit project. If the Chinese-built jetties go ahead first, it is unclear what role remains for the Indian project.
- **Chinese presence close to the border.** Taken with the Teesta plan near the Siliguri Corridor and Chinese interest in Bangladesh's ports, the project extends China's footprint in infrastructure along India's eastern flank. The CRCC memorandum's broad list of sectors (energy, transport, logistics, industrial zones) and Rahman's plan for a Mongla-to-Panchagarh corridor point to more Chinese-backed work running north towards the border with north Bengal. No such project has been announced.

## What they are saying

At the ceremony, Rahman said the project would "help strengthen the country's industry, trade and economic security", reports said. He described Mongla as a future economic hub for Bangladesh's south-west and north-west. He said the government would improve road links between Mongla and Panchagarh, Bangladesh's northernmost district, which borders north Bengal. He also promised to move quickly to supply enough power and gas for economic activity from Mongla to the north. Once the project is complete, he said, container trains will run directly from the Kamalapur inland container depot in Dhaka to the port.

The port authority's chairman told reporters that attracting cargo and shipping lines, better road links and year-round navigability were key to the project paying off.

China has presented its projects in Bangladesh as development cooperation open to all parties. Liu said in Dhaka on Wednesday that China does "not draw ideological lines". India's Ministry of External Affairs has not commented on the Mongla project. At its briefing on 3 November it said India wanted "constructive" ties with Dhaka.

## What happens next

Construction is due to start now and end by December 2028. The CRCC memorandum sets out areas for cooperation, not specific projects, so the next thing to watch is whether it produces signed contracts or loans, and where. The Panchagarh road plan is not yet a project with a budget or timetable. The next fixed date in India-Bangladesh relations is 12 December, when the 1996 Ganges water-sharing treaty expires; the two sides have not yet set a date for talks on renewing it.
